fact_en:
What is cotton?

Cotton is the soft, white fiber growing around the seeds of the cotton plant. It is pulled and twisted into thread!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang cotton?

Ang cotton mao ang humok, puti nga hibla nga motubo sa palibot sa mga liso sa tanom nga gapas. Kini ginalubid aron mahimong hilo!

findings.note: Body: "Kini ginalubid aron mahimong hilo!" for "twisted into thread". In Cebuano hilo = POISON (this same batch uses it that way in ffct-15388, "makahilong carbon monoxide"); Cebuano for thread is tanod (used correctly in ffct-15429, "mahimong taas nga tanod"). A child reads that cotton is twisted "to become poison", and nothing in the card corrects it. This is the punchline sentence of the card.

fact_en:
How long is the thread inside a silkworm cocoon?

A single silkworm cocoon is made from just one continuous silk thread that can be nearly a kilometer long when unwound!
fact_bis:
Unsa ka gitas-on ang hibla sa sulod sa cocoon sa silkworm?

Ang usa ka cocoon sa silkworm hinimo gikan sa usa ka tuloy-tuloy nga hibla sa seda nga halos usa ka kilometro ang gitas-on kon bukharon!

findings.note: title_bis "Hilo sa Kokon" for "Cocoon Thread" — headline reads as "Poison in the Cocoon" in Cebuano. The body never repeats the word (it uses hibla sa seda), so the title's wrong thing is never corrected; same false friend as ffct-15423.

fact_en:
Did you know copper can kill germs?

Yes! Copper kills many germs that land on it. That's why it's used on door handles people touch a lot!
fact_bis:
Nahibalo ba ka nga makapatay sa mikrobyo ang kobre?

Oo! Ang kobre makapatay sa daghang mikrobyo nga mutugpa niini. Mao nga gigamit kini sa mga kuptanan nga sagad hikapon!

findings.note: title_bis "Tanso Mamatay sa Mikrobyo" reverses the fact: 'mamatay' is intransitive 'will die', so the headline reads 'copper dies from germs' — the opposite of title_en 'Copper Kills Germs'. Needs the transitive form (e.g. 'Tanso Makapatay og Mikrobyo' / 'Pamatay sa Mikrobyo'). The headline is the first thing a child sees and states the relationship backwards.

fact_en: Diffusion stops spreading when particles are evenly balanced on both sides, a state called equilibrium!
fact_bis: Mohunong ang diffusion kon managsama na ang gidaghanon sa mga tipik sa duha ka kilid, gitawag kini ug equilibrium!

findings.note: title_bis "Diffusion sa Bali" for 'Diffusion Reaches Balance'. 'Bali' is the confirmed false friend — in Cebuano it means BROKEN / a fracture (Tagalog 'or rather'), not balance; balance is 'timbang' / 'balanse'. The headline reads 'diffusion of broken'; the equilibrium idea only appears in the body.

fact_en:
Why do water drops form perfect little spheres?

The surface of water has a thin "skin" called surface tension, which is why water drops pull into round beads!
fact_bis:
Nganong magporma og lingin ang mga tulo sa tubig?

Ang ibabaw sa tubig adunay nipis nga "panit" nga gitawag og surface tension, mao nga magtipon nga lingin ang mga tulo sa tubig!

findings.note: title_en 'Round Water Drops' vs title_bis 'Libog Patak Tubig'. 'Libog' means confusion/bewilderment — this same corpus uses it that way in its only other two occurrences (ffct-04232 'Libog sa Tunog Atubang ug Luyo' = confusing sound, ffct-36455 'ang libog nga sentence' = a tangled sentence), and in Tagalog it is a crude word. Round is 'lingin' (254 corpus cards), which this card's own body uses correctly ('magporma og lingin', 'magtipon nga lingin') and the tl title says 'Bilog na Patak Tubig'. The headline a child sees names a different thing entirely.

fact_en:
How do you know if food has spoiled?

You can usually tell when it smells bad, feels slimy, or changes its color!
fact_bis:
Unsaon nimo pagsayod kung daot na ang pagkaon?

Kasagaran makabalo ka kung mahinongdan, manghulas, o mausab na ang kolor niini!

findings.note: EN answer lists three signs of spoilage: 'smells bad, feels slimy, or changes its color'; BIS gives 'mahinongdan, manghulas, o mausab na ang kolor'. 'Mahinongdan' is a one-off in the whole 49k pool — the stem 'hinongdan' appears 0 times, while 'hinungdan' (cause/reason) appears on 630 cards, so it reads as 'becomes a cause', not 'smells bad' (tl has 'mabaho'). Smell is the primary way a child detects spoiled food and it is never stated anywhere in the Cebuano. MEDIUM confidence: the other two signs survive ('manghulas' is defensible as slimy/slippery — the corpus uses 'hulas' for a slippery fish in ffct-28054 — and the colour change is intact), so the question is partly answerable.

fact_en:
Why does food spoil if we can't see anything on it?

Food spoils because tiny living things like bacteria and mold grow on it, even though we cannot see them with our eyes!
fact_bis:
Nganong madunot ang pagkaon bisan walay makita nato?

Madunot ang pagkaon tungod kay nagdaghan niini ang gagmay nga mga buhing butang sama sa bakterya ug agup-op nga dili makita sa mata!

findings.note: title_en 'Why Food Spoils' vs title_bis 'Ngano Mabuak ang Pagkaon'. 'Mabuak' is break/crack — all 132 corpus uses are breaking (bird bones, turtle shells, blood vessels, tree bark), never spoiling. Spoil in this corpus is 'madunot'/'madaot', which this card's own body uses twice ('Nganong madunot ang pagkaon...') and the tl title says 'Nasisira'. The title tells a child the card is about food cracking, not rotting.

fact_en: Soot is that fine black powder — mostly pure carbon — that forms when fuel can't burn completely because there's not enough oxygen around.
fact_bis: Ang agiw (soot) maoy pino nga itom nga pulbos — halos puro nga carbon — nga maporma kung dili hingpit nga masunog ang sugnod tungod kay kulang ang oxygen.

findings.note: title_en "Soot" -> title_bis "Uling". Uling is CHARCOAL, not soot; Cebuano soot is agiw, which this card's own body uses ("Ang agiw (soot) maoy pino nga itom nga pulbos"). The corpus itself proves the split: 86 uses of uling, all charcoal (e.g. ffct-15404 "Charcoal from Wood" -> "Uling Gikan sa Kahoy", ffct-15405 "Uling vs Kahoy", ffct-17128 "Paghimo og Uling"), against 7 uses of agiw, all soot. This card is the outlier. A child meets the same headline word "Uling" elsewhere in the deck meaning the black lumps you cook with, then here it is the one-word title of the card that DEFINES soot, so the headline says charcoal is the fine black powder from incomplete combustion. Defect is confined to the title (body is correct) - same shape as the gold FLAG ffct-15087. Note: uling is correct for charcoal corpus-wide; only the soot reading is wrong.

fact_en: Fog is actually a colloid called an aerosol, made of tiny water droplets suspended in the air!
fact_bis: Ang gabon usa ka kolloid nga aerosol, gihimo sa gagmay nga tulo sa tubig nga nagsabit sa hangin!

findings.note: title_en "Fog an Aerosol Colloid" -> title_bis "Hamog Aerosol nga Colloid". Cebuano for fog is gabon - which this card's own body uses ("Ang gabon usa ka kolloid nga aerosol") - while hamog/yamog is DEW. Corpus check: gabon 46 uses, all fog; yamog 27 uses, all dew; hamog 28 uses, overwhelmingly dew/frost (ffct-18294 "Dew Point sa Hamog", ffct-20488 "Hamog Condensed Water Vapor", ffct-21058 frost). The deck teaches dew and fog as different things, and ffct-15865 in this very batch titles a dew card "Yamog sa Dahon" - one letter from "Hamog" - so the headline tells a child that DEW is the aerosol colloid of droplets suspended in air. Title-confined; lower confidence than the uling row because Philippine usage sometimes stretches hamog to morning mist.

fact_en:
Why do water, oil, and honey flow differently?

Because each liquid has its own unique viscosity!
fact_bis:
Nganong magkalahi modagayday ang tubig, lana, ug dugos?

Tungod kay matag likido adunay kaugalingong viscosity!

findings.note: title_bis "Tubig ug Pukyut" (title_en "Each Liquid Flows Own"). Pukyut/pukyutan is the Tagalog bee word; in Cebuano putyokan = HONEYBEE, so the headline reads "Water and Honeybee". The card is about water, oil and honey (body correctly uses dugos) and never mentions an insect; the title names a different thing and also drops oil.

fact_en: Bonding explains why atoms combine in fixed amounts! In water, it's always two hydrogen to one oxygen because each atom seeks a stable number of electrons.
fact_bis: Ang bonding nagpasabot ngano nga ang mga atoms magtipon sa tino nga gidaghanon! Sa tubig, kanunayng duha ka hydrogen sa usa ka oxygen kay ang matag atom mangita og lig-on nga gidaghanon sa electrons.

findings.note: title_bis "Bonding Pirmi Dose Tubig" for "Bonds Fixed Ratios". In Cebuano dose is the everyday Spanish-derived numeral TWELVE (alas dose), so the headline reads "bonding always twelve, water" — a number that is not in the card and conflicts with the 2-hydrogen-to-1-oxygen fact in the body. Cebuano for ratio/proportion is proporsiyon (already in terms).

fact_en:
Ever wonder why shiny silver turns dark and dull over time?

It happens because silver reacts with sulfur-containing gases floating in the air!
fact_bis:
Natinghala ka ba ngano nga ang nindot nga plata nahimong itom o moluspad?

Mahitabo kini tungod kay ang plata motubag sa mga gas nga adunay asupre sa hangin!

findings.note: title_bis "Pilak Itom Asupre Hangin" uses Tagalog pilak (silver). In Cebuano pilak is the verb to THROW AWAY / discard (ipilak); silver as a metal is plata — which is exactly what the body uses. Headline names no substance at all, so the tarnish card loses its subject in the line a child reads first. Lower confidence than the other two: pilak survives as "silver/money" in some Visayan usage.
